parts: Development is change for the better (social or economic improvement). Development communication is the use of communication to promote development, using interpersonal, group and mass communication and messages designed to change behaviour and improve quality of life. Those who write or produce programmes on development issues are development communicators. A development communicator must understand the process of development and communication, know professional techniques and the audience, and prepare and distribute messages so that they are received, understood, accepted and applied.

History: rural radio broadcasts in the 1940s in local languages (farming, interviews with experts, folk songs, weather, market rates, improved seeds). Doordarshan started on 15 September 1959 concentrating on agriculture (Krishi Darshan). In 1975 SITE (Satellite Instructional Television Experiment) made education and development programmes available to 2400 villages in Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Rajasthan. Print media gave importance to development themes after the Five Year Plans. Radio and television (AIR and Doordarshan) carry development messages. Traditional media are closest to the people who need the messages (farmers, workers); they are participatory and effective: street theatre with humorous skits (balanced nutrition for construction workers, literacy, hygiene) and locally made comics (story telling with visuals in local language and culture; used for HIV/AIDS in several states). Development communication needs development agencies (e.g. agriculture departments), voluntary organizations, concerned citizens and NGOs.

Agriculture, fisheries, animal husbandry, food security, communication, irrigation, public works, employment, environment, ecology, income generation activities, education, health and sanitation, family welfare. Expertise comes from agricultural colleges, state agriculture, horticulture and fisheries departments, soil testing laboratories, Krishi Bhawans, Community Development Blocks, Primary Health Centres and NGOs.

A campaign uses communication over a period to bring change, like an election campaign (public meetings, print, radio and TV advertising). Development examples: monthly polio immunization day and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (elementary education for all children aged 6–14 with community participation). Communicators must understand the audience and its needs and present messages attractively. Rural India still needs government support, so government communication remains significant; Public Information campaigns in villages encourage local participation.
